nstead of suing manufacturers directly, individuals who believe they’ve been injured by a vaccine can file a claim through the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP). This program provides compensation for rare vaccine-related injuries and is funded by a small tax on vaccines. If a claim through the VICP is denied or the individual is unsatisfied with the compensation, they still have the option to pursue a lawsuit against the vaccine manufacturer in civil court, but only under very limited circumstances. These cases are rare and typically require proving that the manufacturer was negligent or that the vaccine was defective in some way. The system is designed to balance protecting vaccine manufacturers to encourage vaccine development while still offering a pathway for people to seek justice if they suffer harm. However, most vaccine injury claims are resolved through the VICP, which aims to provide faster and more accessible compensation than traditional lawsuits.

@thehabit4373  No, it’s not just because the doctor "read and studied" or because they went to college and can “read better.” It’s because medicine is an extraordinarily vast and layered field that requires years of rigorous and structured learning. Not just memorization, but deep, critical understanding.  Medicine is built on an interconnected hierarchy of sciences. You can’t understand diseases without a solid foundation in pathology, but you can’t grasp pathology unless you understand physiology. And to truly comprehend physiology, you need to start even further back, with cell biology, biochemistry, and anatomy, the very building blocks of life and the human body.  Each subject builds on the previous one. For instance, you won’t make sense of pharmacology, without understanding physiology and biochemistry. You need to know how the liver metabolizes medications, how receptors function, how systems interact. And that’s just the basic sciences. the “preclinical” stage.  After that, we move into clinical sciences, where everything becomes even more complex. Here we start seeing real patients with real problems, and we learn that diseases don’t always present like they do in textbooks. Medicine is often unpredictable. Patients can have subtle, atypical symptoms or multiple overlapping conditions. This is why clinical experience is crucial. It trains us to think critically, to recognize patterns, and to expect the unexpected.  Many people assume medicine is just about memorizing vast amounts of information. And yes, we do memorize a lot, but that’s only a part of it. What really matters is understanding. We have to make sense of deeply interconnected biological systems, interpret diagnostic tests, and use that understanding to reason through a patient's symptoms. It’s not enough to know that a drug works, we have to know why it works, when to use it, and what could go wrong.  So no, doctors aren’t just people who studied a bit more in college. They go through years of specialized training, mastering foundational sciences, learning to think like clinicians, and then spending thousands of hours applying that knowledge to real-life human beings.
